children: By Mark R. Long

Lineage, the world's No. 1 cold-storage operator by capacity, is suing solar-panel provider Altus Power and contractor Pearce Services, alleging their negligence caused a fire that destroyed a Los Angeles warehouse.

The WSJ Logistics Report's Liz Young writes that the fire started June 17 at the 500,000-square-foot, temperature-controlled warehouse in the Boyle Heights neighborhood and smoldered for days. The building was storing millions of pounds of fresh and frozen food such as meat, bread and seafood that rotted after the blaze, prompting complaints, citations and lawsuits over foul odors and pests.

The suit says Altus, owned by private-equity firm TPG, leased the building's roof from Lineage to own and operate a solar-panel array, and that Altus hired Pearce to conduct maintenance on the panels. Lineage said the fire started while Pearce employees were working on the array.

Los Palos Street Operating, a subsidiary of Altus Power, and Pearce, a unit of commercial real-estate company (CBRE Group) denied Lineage's claims and said they plan to contest the accusations in court.

Demand for industrial real estate, as measured by square footage of net absorption-the amount of newly occupied space minus the amount vacated-in the first half of 2026, up around 80% from the same period last year, according to Colliers.
Maritime Security

Iran-backed Houthi militants seized a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait and a town along its mainland coast on Friday, the Journal reports. The advance gives the Yemeni rebels effective control of one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints after a rapid offensive.

The Houthis took control of Perim Island, Saudi and Yemeni officials said. The volcanic island sits inside the Bab al-Mandeb and divides the narrow waterway into two shipping channels, giving whoever holds it a powerful position to threaten vessels entering or leaving the Red Sea. The militants also reached the Yemeni town of Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait.
The seizures cap a series of swift Houthi gains. The militants captured the strategic port city of Mokha on Thursday and are pushing along other stretches of Yemen's Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia's oil production fell 23% in August to 6.24 million barrels a day, as Houthi rebel threats disrupted west coast exports.
OPEC cut its forecast for global oil-demand growth this year to 380,000 barrels a day, down from its previous estimate of 580,000 barrels a day. (WSJ)
Iran has resumed production of missiles, assembling them from stored components despite significant disruption to its manufacturing base and supply chain. (WSJ)
Somali pirates reportedly seized the bulk carrier Glamor in the Gulf of Aden, the latest in a string of recent attacks on commercial vessels. (Lloyd's List)
Air Cargo

The deadly crash of an Amazon cargo plane has brought attention to the little-known freight carrier operating the flight-21 Air-and its well-known owner, Jim Crane, the logistics magnate and owner of the Houston Astros baseball team.

The WSJ's Andrew Tangel and Hanna Krueger write that 21 Air flies for carriers such as Amazon and DHL Express and has expanded rapidly. It has also left a trail of complaints from former employees who alleged problems with the airline's safety culture.

The airline's safety practices, its arrangement with Amazon and the pilots' actions are among the National Transportation Safety Board's lines of inquiry into the Miami incident that killed five people. 21 Air said safety has been core to the company since 2021, when Crane acquired a controlling stake. An Amazon spokesman said the retailer's operating partners are certified by federal air-safety regulators, and compared the arrangement with how U.S. passenger carriers contract with regional airlines.

Since Crane bought the carrier, it has faced complaints from former employees over how it handled safety. Among them, a former chief pilot testified in a federal whistleblower case that the airline's safety director told him not to file his concerns. The company disputed the allegations.
"Does Amazon just take a hands-off approach? Do they evaluate these operators? We don't know."NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy
In Other News

Wholesale-price inflation sped up in August, with the producer-price index rising by 0.4%, up from a 0.1% increase in July, the Labor Department said. Over the 12 months through August, producer-price inflation was 5.4%. (WSJ)

The transportation equipment PPI rose 2.6% year over year in August, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics said, with the sector's services PPI rising 7.6% for air, 1.4% for rail, 14.3% for trucking and 16.7% for water.
Existing home sales in August fell to their lowest level in more than a year, and interest rates on a 30-year fixed mortgage topped 7%, also for the first time in over a year. (WSJ)
Macy's raised its full-year outlook, which executives said was partly driven by higher prices on its products. (WSJ)
Chemours, DuPont and Corteva reached a $455 million settlement with North Carolina and 11 communities over drinking-water toxins. (WSJ)
Safelite's U.K.-based owner Belron is exploring strategic options for the business, including a potential stock market listing. (WSJ)
A fire aboard a cargo ship under repair at the Chinese state-owned Qingdao Beihai shipyard killed 25 people. (Reuters)
A.P. Moller-Maersk is planning to order up to 42 newly built ships in a nearly $9 billion fleet expansion. (TradeWinds)
Wiwynn, which makes server systems and racks for Amazon, is investing more than $1.6 billion in its manufacturing plant in Socorro, Texas. (SupplyChain247)
BNSF Railway, Canadian Pacific Kansas City, and CSX are planning to seek access to a combined Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern system if regulators approve their proposed merger. (TrainsPRO)
Ford Motor said it would invest $1 billion in a new paint shop at its Kentucky Truck Plant. (Louisville Business First)
